overview:
In 1206 a council of steppe leaders on the Onon River confirmed Temüjin, a man who had spent his early life among the losing side of Mongolia's tribal feuds, as ruler of all the Mongols under the title Genghis Khan. What followed was expansion at a speed with few parallels. Within a generation Mongol armies had broken the Jin dynasty in northern China, obliterated the Khwarazmian state in Central Asia, and ridden through the Caucasus into the Rus' principalities. Under Genghis's son Ögedei the pressure continued: the Jin fell in 1234, Kievan Rus' was subdued by 1240, and raiding columns reached Hungary and Poland before the campaign was broken off. His grandson Hülegü took Baghdad in 1258 and ended the Abbasid caliphate; another grandson, Kublai, completed the conquest of Song China by 1276, the first time a non-Chinese power had held the whole country. At its greatest reach it was the largest contiguous land empire there has ever been, running from the Pacific to the edge of Europe.

The machinery behind this mattered as much as the cavalry. Commands were handed out by demonstrated competence rather than birth alone, conquered specialists — Chinese engineers, Persian administrators, Uyghur scribes — were absorbed into the apparatus, and the major religions were largely left to operate untaxed and unmolested so long as their clergy prayed for the khan. A relay post system, the yam, moved messengers and orders across thousands of miles of grassland. The result was a period sometimes called the Pax Mongolica, in which merchants, envoys, friars and craftsmen moved between China, Iran and the Mediterranean along routes that had never been so continuously open — and along which, in the 1340s, plague appears to have travelled too.

Unity did not last. Möngke's death in 1259 left no agreed successor, and the war between his brothers Kublai and Ariq Böke settled into a permanent split. The defeat at Ain Jalut in 1260 marked the western limit of expansion in the Middle East, and by the end of the century the empire functioned as four separate states: Kublai's Yuan dynasty in China, the Ilkhanate in Iran, the Chagatai khanate in Central Asia, and the Golden Horde on the Russian steppe. They fought each other as readily as outsiders. The Yuan was driven out of China by the Ming in 1368, the conventional end date for the empire as a whole, though the successor khanates and their offshoots persisted for centuries afterwards.
significance: The Mongol century pulled Eurasia into a single, if brutal, circuit of exchange. Ideas and goods that had moved slowly and indirectly — gunpowder weaponry, printing, Chinese medical and astronomical knowledge, Persian historiography and cartography — crossed the continent under one set of political protections, and Europeans acquired a far more concrete picture of Asia than they had ever had. The empire also rewrote political geography: it ended the Abbasid caliphate, brought China under a foreign dynasty that its Ming successors would define themselves against, shaped the emergence of Muscovy under and then out of the Golden Horde, and left a template of steppe legitimacy that rulers from Timur to the Mughals and the Qing would still be invoking centuries later. Genghisid descent remained a claim worth making long after the empire itself was gone.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all for the Mongol Empire, so nothing here comes from the map's own records — it is written from general reference works. Two gaps in the wider record are worth naming: the Mongols left little writing of their own beyond the Secret History of the Mongols, composed around 1228–29 and revised later, so most of what we know is filtered through Persian, Chinese, Arabic, Armenian and Latin authors, many of them writing about their own conquerors. And the casualty figures often quoted — tens of millions — rest on medieval chronicle numbers that specialists regard as inflated, sometimes by an order of magnitude, and on population estimates for the period that are themselves guesses; the scale of the destruction was real, but the arithmetic is not.
